title: The Garments in Which the Soul Goes Forth, and the Concord of Principles That Must Clothe It
reading:
When the Divine Human goes forth toward the proprium, he goes clothed; and what does the work within that clothing is divine love itself. Love alone is enough — one principle, by itself, suffices to quench the proprium's foolishness and to bring down its arrogance through the whole expanse where self-love spreads itself out. Yet because love is to operate within the natural, the life-bearing principle in the Lord provides four further accommodations to attend it as helpers: thought, truth in the natural degree, wisdom in receivable form, and the medium of perception. These four are given to surround love and to bring its work to completion, so that what stands against the Lord may be cut off.

In doing this work love itself takes a wound. Divine love accommodating itself into the lower degree suffers there; this is the cost of its going forth, and on account of this wound all the particular forms of the proprium are constrained. The other accommodations too take their share of suffering as they enter the contest. The proprium does not join with them and cannot be joined with them; its burning cannot encircle them. Yet one among them — the medium of perception, which alone was not pierced — was stripped of its outer form, and another vesture was given in its place. Clothed now in this living medium, the four hold together and prevail, and become for the soul the dwelling-place of life.

For this is the order of the Lord's principles: they dwell together with one another forever in concord; not one of them transgresses against the order, not one steps outside the message that another gives to it, not one becomes like the darkness. The proprium is the opposite of this. It is one of a single practice — self-loving practice — and that practice is itself alone, with no companion but itself. The kingdom of self-love is in this same way one principle, herself alone; she has no fellow because her practice admits of none.

Those whose interior states follow the Lord's pattern leave their deep behind them and come up, rising after the one whom the Lord has appointed, because the same practice — the practice of receiving and not claiming — exists in them all. They scatter the darkness; they humble the proprium's particular forms. So long as the soul's inner states agree with one another under the Lord's order, doing honor to that order, they receive glory in proportion to what they have received, and are exalted far above the kingdom of self-love that rose up against them. But wherever the soul's inner states fall out with one another and side with the proprium against the order, they must by necessity perish in that kingdom of self-love; they fall into humblings, and they come at last under the hand of the very order that stood against them.
